claim: Article 12: in Part III, 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, judgment 13 Nov 1980 (five judges), Supreme Court official copy (api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/4414.pdf)
note: Part III binds 'the State' in this wide sense, not only the Government. gees2 ch.6 (Grade 7) uses 'State' in the political-science sense; that is a different use of the word.

claim: Ajay Hasia (13 Nov 1980, five judges, judgment by Bhagwati J.): a body that acts as an instrumentality or agency of the Government can be an 'authority' under Article 12, so Part III binds it.
source: Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, judgment 13 Nov 1980 (five judges), Supreme Court official copy (api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/4414.pdf)
page_or_section: Bhagwati J. (sole judgment for the Bench of five), judis PDF p.4: tests for an instrumentality or agency of the State
note: Indian Kanoon copy of the SCR text; court copy not reached. Wording of the full test (six factors) not checked. AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: official copy obtained and read; bench Chandrachud CJ, Bhagwati, Krishna Iyer, Fazal Ali, Koshal JJ; one judgment, by Bhagwati J. The Indian Kanoon copy is no longer needed. Rows beyond the general instrumentality-or-agency idea (the six-factor test) are still not claimed.

claim: Article 13(1): laws in force in India immediately before the Constitution began are void to the extent they are inconsistent with Part III.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: Article 13(2): the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the rights in Part III; a law made against this is void to the extent of the contravention.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.28 gives the same idea in plain words (rights protected by the Constitution itself; no organ of government may violate them).

claim: Article 13(3)(a): 'law' in Article 13 includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, and custom or usage having the force of law in India. (UPSC Prelims 2026 Q54: both speakers' points are in this text.)
value: ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: PYQ link. The question's speaker X lists ordinances, orders, rules and regulations; speaker Y adds custom or usage. Both are in the clause, so an option calling Y's view wrong would be wrong. Answer options were read only as OCR (research/upsc/_pyq/ocr/2026_prelims_gs1-29.pgm.txt), so the exact letter is not recorded here.

claim: Article 13(3)(b): 'laws in force' includes laws made before the Constitution began and not repealed, even if not then in operation everywhere.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: Article 13(4) says nothing in Article 13 applies to an amendment made under Article 368. It was inserted by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971 (in force 5 Nov 1971).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Supreme Court of India, Basic Structure Judgment site: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (SCR text), reused from POL-06
note: Cross-reference POL-06 (claims POL06-A04, B01, D04, D05). In Kesavananda (1973) ten judges held an amendment is not 'law' under Art. 13(2) (Golaknath overruled), but seven judges held Parliament cannot alter the basic structure. Not repeated in depth here.

claim: Kesavananda Bharati (24 Apr 1973): ten judges held that 'law' in Article 13(2) does not cover constitutional amendments; seven held the amending power cannot alter the basic structure. So Part III can be amended, but not so as to destroy the basic structure.
value: 10 judges on Art 13(2); 7 judges on basic structure
source: Supreme Court of India, Basic Structure Judgment site: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (SCR text), reused from POL-06
second_source: Reused claim ids POL06-D04, POL06-D05 (audited 2 Nov 2026)
note: Reused from POL-06 without re-reading the judgment. Say 'seven judges on this question', not '7-6 verdict'. Details in POL-06.

claim: Article 123(3): an Ordinance that makes a provision Parliament could not enact under the Constitution is void. Together with Art. 13(3)(a), an Ordinance cannot take away a Part III right. (Prelims 2025 asked whether an Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right.)
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Inference from two articles; the Prelims 2025 statement was read from OCR (research/upsc/_pyq/2025_prelims_gs1.txt). Art. 123(3) text located by search.

claim: Some rights are for every 'person': Article 14 (equality before law) says 'any person'; Article 21 (life and liberty) says 'No person'.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Foreigners in India can use these rights.

claim: Some rights are for 'citizens' only: Article 19 begins 'All citizens shall have the right'; Articles 15, 16 and 29(1) are also written for citizens.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Article 25 says 'All persons'; Article 30 says 'All minorities'.

claim: NCERT Grade 8 says fundamental rights are 'basic rights that every Indian citizen has'. The Constitution's text is narrower and wider at once: some Part III rights are for every person (Art. 14 'any person'; Arts 20, 21, 22 'no person' or 'every person'; Art. 25 'all persons'; Art. 27 'no person'), Art. 21A is for 'all children' aged six to fourteen, Art. 26 is for 'every religious denomination', Arts 23 and 24 are written as prohibitions with no limit to citizens, and others are only for citizens (Arts 15, 16, 19, 29).
source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch.5 Citizenship: Rights and Duties (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: NCERT simplifies. The corrected statement rests on the article texts (A10, A11, F01). Arts 20-24 verified by text search in F-group and D/E-group claims.

claim: Article 14: the State shall not deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within India.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
note: NCERT iest1 p.141 gives the plain-words split: equality before law = no one above the law; equal protection = people in like situations treated alike.

claim: NCERT Grade 9 explains the two phrases: 'equality before law' (everyone treated equally by the law whatever their rank) and 'equal protection of law' (people in similar circumstances treated equally, without arbitrary discrimination).
source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: Indra Sawhney v Union of India, judgment 16 Nov 1992 (nine judges), copy of the Supreme Court Reports text on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: Indra Sawhney (lead judgment, para 5) notes both phrases appear in Art. 14 though most constitutions use only one.

claim: Maneka Gandhi (25 Jan 1978): Bhagwati J. (for himself, Untwalia and Fazal Ali JJ.), quoting the Royappa case, wrote that equality is opposed to arbitrariness and that Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness in State action.
source: Supreme Court of India: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, judgment 25 Jan 1978 (seven judges)
note: Bhagwati J.'s opinion is the lead opinion; Beg CJ, Chandrachud J. and Krishna Iyer J. concurred; Kailasam J. dissented (headnote list). The Royappa quote is the Court quoting itself.

claim: Article 15(1): the State shall not discriminate against a citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 15(2): no citizen shall, on those grounds only, face a disability about shops, hotels, restaurants, entertainment places, wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads or places of public resort.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Social and Political Life II, Class VII, ch.1 On Equality (2024-25 printing)
note: Clause (2) is written as 'No citizen shall', not 'the State shall not'. Our reading (inference): it reaches private shopkeepers too. NCERT gess3 p.8 prints the same text. NCERT keps2 p.31 tea-shop example.

claim: Article 15(3) lets the State make special provisions for women and children. Article 15(4), added by the First Amendment (in force 18 Jun 1951), lets it make special provision for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Indra Sawhney v Union of India, judgment 16 Nov 1992 (nine judges), copy of the Supreme Court Reports text on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: Indra Sawhney paras 28, 56 link clause (4) to State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan (1951); that case was not opened itself.

claim: Article 15(5), inserted by the 93rd Amendment (in force 20 Jan 2006): special provisions for admission to educational institutions, including private aided or unaided ones, other than minority institutions under Article 30(1).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: Articles 15(6) and 16(6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment (in force 14 Jan 2019): special provision for economically weaker sections (other than SC/ST/backward classes already covered), up to a maximum of ten per cent, in addition to existing reservations.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
page_or_section: Art. 15(6), 16(6); footnote 3 on Art. 15; PDF p.38
second_source: Supreme Court of India: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India, WP(C) 55/2019, judgment 7 Nov 2022 (five judges)
note: 'Economically weaker sections' are to be notified by the State on the basis of family income and other indicators of disadvantage (Explanation).

claim: Article 16(1)-(2): equality of opportunity in public employment; no citizen may be ineligible or discriminated against only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. Article 16(3) lets Parliament require residence for some posts.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.30-31 summarises the same.

claim: Article 16(4): nothing in Article 16 stops the State from reserving appointments or posts for any backward class of citizens which, in the State's opinion, is not adequately represented in State services. NCERT prints this text and says it shows reservation is not a violation of equality.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.32 (box) and p.33. 'In the opinion of the State' and 'not adequately represented' are the two tests the Court later worked on (Indra Sawhney).

claim: Article 16(4A) (77th Amendment, in force 17 Jun 1995): reservation in promotion for SCs and STs not adequately represented. Article 16(4B) (81st Amendment, in force 9 Jun 2000): unfilled reserved vacancies of a year are carried forward and not counted in that year's 50% ceiling.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Indra Sawhney, para 121(7): Art. 16(4) did not permit reservation in promotion (IK copy)
note: Order of events: Indra Sawhney (16 Nov 1992) held no reservation in promotion; the 77th Amendment added 16(4A) in 1995. The 85th Amendment (2001) added 'consequential seniority' retrospectively from 17-6-1995 (footnote 3).

claim: Article 17: 'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden; enforcing any disability arising from it is an offence punishable in accordance with law.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Social and Political Life III, Class VIII, ch.6 Confronting Marginalisation / ch.7 Public Facilities (2024-25 printing)
note: NCERT hess3 p.75. The law that punishes it is the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; its text was BLOCKED (indiacode.nic.in returned 504 on 3 Nov 2026), see open items.

claim: Article 18: the State shall confer no title, other than a military or academic distinction; a citizen may not accept a title from a foreign State.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.31. The Court's ruling that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not 'titles' (1996) was not retrieved.

claim: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (No. 33 of 1989, 11 Sep 1989) lists acts such as forcing a member of an SC or ST to eat or drink an inedible or obnoxious substance as offences. NCERT quotes the same list.
source: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (No. 33 of 1989), original text, Ministry of Tribal Affairs
second_source: NCERT Social and Political Life III, Class VIII, ch.6 Confronting Marginalisation / ch.7 Public Facilities (2024-25 printing)
note: Original 1989 text from the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. The Act was later amended (an Amendment Act in 2015, in force Jan 2016, and one in 2018); the consolidated text could not be read (indiacode 504). Dated item. FOLLOW-UP 3-4 Nov 2026: the consolidated text is now read (X07): the 2015 Amendment Act (Act 1 of 2016) came into force 26-1-2016 and the 2018 Amendment Act (27 of 2018) on 20-8-2018. B13 itself (the 1989 list of offences) is unchanged.

source: Indra Sawhney v Union of India, judgment 16 Nov 1992 (nine judges), copy of the Supreme Court Reports text on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)

claim: Jarnail Singh (26 Sep 2018, five judges: Misra CJI, Joseph, Nariman, Kaul, Malhotra JJ.): Nagaraj does not need a seven-judge bench, but its requirement to collect quantifiable data on backwardness of SCs and STs is invalid, as it conflicts with Indra Sawhney.
value: no data on SC/ST backwardness needed for promotion quota
source: Jarnail Singh v Lachhmi Narain Gupta, SLP(C) 30621/2011 etc., judgment 26 Sep 2018 (Constitution Bench, five judges), Supreme Court of India, own copy
page_or_section: para 14, PDF p.40; para 21, PDF p.57-58; signature block Misra CJI, Joseph, Nariman, Kaul, Malhotra, PDF p.58
note: Official copy read 3 Nov 2026. One unanimous judgment, written by R.F. Nariman J. (heading 'R.F. Nariman, J.'). Para 21: Nagaraj need not go to seven judges; its holding that the State must collect quantifiable data showing backwardness of SCs and STs is contrary to the nine-judge Indra Sawhney and is held invalid to that extent. Para 14 says the same at greater length. The State must still collect quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation in the cadre (PDF p.48). The IK-only caveat is closed. The creamy-layer discussion in this judgment (paras 11-13 in the old note) was not read in full.

claim: Dr Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil (5 May 2021, five judges): Indra Sawhney needs no reference to a larger bench and no reconsideration; the 12-13% Maratha reservation added to the existing 50% was not justified by 'exceptional circumstances' (Bhat J., conclusions para 188, agreeing with Bhushan J.).
value: 50% ceiling kept; Maratha quota beyond it not justified
source: Supreme Court of India: Dr Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v Chief Minister, Maharashtra, CA 3123/2020, judgment 5 May 2021 (five judges)
second_source: Indra Sawhney v Union of India, judgment 16 Nov 1992 (nine judges), copy of the Supreme Court Reports text on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: Bhushan J. wrote for himself and Nazeer J.; Rao, Gupta and Bhat JJ. concurred on questions 1-3 (cover note of the judgment). The 102nd Amendment question (Art. 342A) was decided separately and by a split (C11).

claim: The 102nd Amendment (2018) added Articles 338B, 342A and 366(26C): the President specifies socially and educationally backward classes by public notification. In Jaishri Patil (2021) Bhat J.'s conclusion was that only the President can identify them; the 105th Amendment (2021) later added Art. 342A(3) so States and Union territories can keep their own lists.
value: President's list; States' power restored by 105th Amendment, 2021
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Supreme Court of India: Dr Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v Chief Minister, Maharashtra, CA 3123/2020, judgment 5 May 2021 (five judges)
note: Bhat J. wrote this conclusion (para 188(4)-(5)(i)-(vii)). Correction (audit 3 Nov 2026): Nageswara Rao J. and Hemant Gupta J. agreed with Bhat J. on Questions 4-6, so this is the 3:2 majority view on the 102nd Amendment; Bhushan J. (for himself and Nazeer J.) took the opposite view (his para 443 approves the High Court's reading that the 102nd Amendment does not take away the State's competence). I read the clause (3) wording through the Constitution footnotes only; the 105th Amendment Act itself was not opened (Art. 342A footnotes: 102nd w.e.f. 15-8-2018; 105th w.e.f. 15-9-2021).

claim: Janhit Abhiyan (7 Nov 2022): by 3:2 the Court upheld the 103rd Amendment (EWS quota). The majority were Maheshwari, Trivedi and Pardiwala JJ.; Bhat J. (for himself and the Chief Justice, Lalit) dissented.
source: Supreme Court of India: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India, WP(C) 55/2019, judgment 7 Nov 2022 (five judges)
page_or_section: Order of the Court, PDF p.1-2; PDF p.2
note: Four separate judgments were delivered: Maheshwari J.; Bhat J. (for himself and the Chief Justice); Trivedi J.; Pardiwala J. (Order). Opinions differ on reasons.

claim: Janhit Abhiyan, Maheshwari J.: ten per cent in addition to existing reservations does not damage the basic structure through breach of the 50% ceiling, because that ceiling is not inflexible and applies only to reservations under Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4).
value: 50% ceiling not inflexible; applies to 15(4), 15(5), 16(4) only
source: Supreme Court of India: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India, WP(C) 55/2019, judgment 7 Nov 2022 (five judges)
page_or_section: Maheshwari J., conclusion paras (before para 104); PDF p.155
note: Attributed to Maheshwari J.'s judgment. The other two majority judges wrote separately and agree in the result; whether each adopts this exact reasoning on the ceiling was not checked.

claim: Janhit Abhiyan, Bhat J. (dissent, for himself and the Chief Justice): Sections 2 and 3 of the 103rd Amendment, which inserted Art. 15(6) and 16(6), violate the basic structure; the poor among SCs, STs and OBCs are excluded from the new quota.
source: Supreme Court of India: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India, WP(C) 55/2019, judgment 7 Nov 2022 (five judges)
note: A minority view. Bhat J. agreed that economic criteria alone may be allowed under Art. 15 but not under Art. 16 (para 193).

claim: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh (1 Aug 2024, seven judges): by 6:1, sub-classification within the Scheduled Castes is allowed under Articles 14, 15(4) and 16(4); the State must show inadequate representation based on data; the 2004 Chinnaiah ruling is overruled. Trivedi J. dissented.
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, CA 2317/2011, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), 2024 INSC 562, Supreme Court of India, own copy
page_or_section: CJI Chandrachud (for himself and Manoj Misra J.), para 205(a)-(f), PDF p.138-139; Trivedi J. dissent, para 80, PDF p.509
note: Official copy read 3 Nov 2026. Para 205 is signed by the CJI and Manoj Misra J.; Gavai J. (para 296 conclusion), Vikram Nath J. (PDF p.422), Pankaj Mithal J. and Satish Chandra Sharma J. wrote concurring opinions agreeing that Chinnaiah is overruled and sub-classification is allowed with empirical data; Trivedi J. holds that Chinnaiah 'is the correct law' (para 80). That is 6:1; say 'majority of six'. 205(f)(i)-(ii): the State must establish that inadequacy of representation is due to backwardness and must collect data on it.

claim: Davinder Singh, Gavai J. (separate concurring opinion, para 295): the State must evolve a policy to identify the creamy layer even among the Scheduled Castes, to take them out of the reservation benefit.
value: creamy layer for SC/ST: Gavai J., agreed by Nath, Mithal and Sharma JJ. (separate opinions)
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, CA 2317/2011, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), 2024 INSC 562, Supreme Court of India, own copy
page_or_section: Gavai J., para 295, PDF p.419; Vikram Nath J., paras 1-2, PDF p.422-423; Pankaj Mithal J., para 83, PDF p.560; Satish Chandra Sharma J., para 2, PDF p.565
note: Official copy read 3 Nov 2026. Para 295 reads 'the State must evolve a policy for identifying the creamy layer even from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes so as exclude them from the benefit of affirmative action.' It is Gavai J.'s separate opinion. Nath J., Mithal J. and Sharma J. each say they agree with it in their own opinions. The conclusions of the CJI and Misra J. (para 205) do not include a creamy-layer holding, so do not call it the Court's holding; say 'four of the seven judges, in separate opinions'. Trivedi J. dissented on the main question.

claim: Article 335: the claims of SCs and STs to services shall be taken into account consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration; a proviso (82nd Amendment, 2000) permits relaxation in qualifying marks or standards in evaluation for reservation in promotion.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, CA 2317/2011, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), copy on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: In Davinder Singh the CJI's opinion says Art. 335 is not a limitation on Arts 16(1), 16(4) but a restatement of the need to consider SC/ST claims (para 205 (f) iii). AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: the claim is the Art. 335 text (Legislative Department, proviso by the 82nd Amendment, w.e.f. 8-9-2000, confirmed). The Davinder Singh para 205(f)(iii) remark is from Indian Kanoon only (official copy not read). FOLLOW-UP 3-4 Nov 2026: official copy of Davinder Singh now read: CJI para 205(f)(iii) says Art. 335 is not a limitation on Arts 16(1) and 16(4) but a restatement of the need to consider SC/ST claims (PDF p.139). The IK-only caveat above is closed.

claim: Article 46 (a Directive Principle): the State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, in particular SCs and STs, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation. NCERT Grade 9 quotes it.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
note: NCERT iest1 p.143.

claim: Articles 341(1) and 342(1): the President, after consulting the Governor, may by public notification specify the castes or tribes to be treated as Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes in a State; Parliament may by law include or exclude (341(2), 342(2)).
value: SC and ST lists: President by notification; Parliament by law
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: So the Scheduled lists are national-law matters, while backward-class lists were left to States until 2018 and again after 2021 (C11).

claim: Article 334 ends the SC/ST seat reservation after eighty years from the Constitution's start (our arithmetic: 25 Jan 2030).
value: seat reservation in legislatures; Art. 334 sunset
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: The text says 'eighty years' for SC/ST seats and 'seventy years' for the other clause. The end date 25 Jan 2030 is our arithmetic (the Constitution began 26 Jan 1950); the 104th Amendment footnote was not individually opened.

claim: Articles 330(2) and 332: the seats reserved for SCs and STs in the House of the People and in each State Assembly bear, as nearly as may be, the same proportion to the total seats as their population bears to the State's population (Art. 330(2)). Jarnail Singh (2018) contrasts this proportional rule with the open wording of Art. 16(4A).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Jarnail Singh v Lachhmi Narain Gupta, judgment 26 Sep 2018 (five judges), copy on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: Jarnail Singh (2018, para 20) draws the contrast between Art. 330 and Art. 16(4A). AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: NCERT does not draw this contrast (no Art. 330 or 16(4A) in the NCERT files); only Jarnail Singh does, in paras 19-20, Indian Kanoon copy.

claim: Women's reservation: the 106th Amendment Act (2023) added Arts 330A, 332A and 334A. The 10 Sep 2026 Constitution prints their footnotes as s.3 (Art. 330A), s.4 (Art. 332A) and s.5 (Art. 334A), each 'w.e.f. 16-4-2026', but the PDF's hidden text layer also carries the words '(date yet to be notified)' over the same footnotes. Art. 334A says the women's seats take effect only after a delimitation done on the first census taken after the Act, and cease after fifteen years.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
page_or_section: Art. 334A; Art. 330A and footnotes; PDF p.224
second_source: Reused claim POL06-A13 (audited 2 Nov 2026)
note: Reused from POL-06 (A13); the footnote wording was re-searched in the 10 Sep 2026 text. Date every use; this is a living fact. AUDIT 3 Nov 2026 correction: the earlier wording 'only its section 4 (Art. 330A) is in force' was wrong. On the page images (PDF p.221, 223, 224) Art. 330A is footnote s.3, Art. 332A is s.4 and Art. 334A is s.5, all 'w.e.f. 16-4-2026'; the text layer adds '(date yet to be notified)' on top, so the Legislative Department's own file is internally unclear. Do not state when the quota starts to operate until the Gazette notification is read. The same slip (s.4 for Art. 330A) is in POL06-A13.

claim: DoPT OM of 22 Oct 1993 (in the compendium; it refers back to the OBC OM of 8 Sep 1993): following Indra Sawhney, SC, ST and OBC reservations together must not exceed 50% of vacancies arising in a year; it also refers to the existing 15% SC and 7.5% ST reservation in all-India open-competition direct recruitment.
source: DoPT, Government of India: Compendium of instructions on reservation for Other Backward Classes (Part III)
page_or_section: OM of 22 Oct 1993, paras 1-2; PDF p.48
second_source: Indra Sawhney para 121(6)
note: The compendium text is an OCR scan and the OM is from 1993. A current DoPT consolidated OM was not downloaded, so 'today's' rates are not confirmed here (see C24). AUDIT 3 Nov 2026 correction: the 50% rule and the 15% SC and 7.5% ST roster rates are in the OM of 22 Oct 1993 (PDF p.48), not in the 8 Sep 1993 OM, which only sets the 27% OBC provision.

claim: EWS in Central Government direct recruitment: DoPT's OM of 31 Jan 2019 provides 10% reservation; the DoPT FAQ describes eligibility by family income (below Rs 8 lakh gross annual) and asset tests.
value: 10% EWS; family income below Rs 8 lakh
source: DoPT, Government of India: FAQ on reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (OM 31.01.2019)
note: Income limit is read from the FAQ; income limits are revised by the Government, so check before use. Date the FAQ at use.

claim: Our arithmetic (inference): 15% SC + 7.5% ST + 27% OBC = 49.5%; adding the 10% EWS quota in Central posts gives 59.5% reserved, which is why 'the 50% rule' now needs the words 'for the classes in 15(4), 15(5), 16(4)'.
as_of: our arithmetic from C02, C22, C23
source: DoPT, Government of India: Compendium of instructions on reservation for Other Backward Classes (Part III)
note: INFERENCE. Not a figure printed in any source. The 15% and 7.5% come from a 1993 OM and were not re-checked at a 2026 DoPT OM, so this stays UNVERIFIED until they are.

claim: NCERT Class 8 says the reservation policy is 'significant and highly contentious': seats in education and government jobs are reserved for Dalits and Adivasis because for centuries they were denied opportunities; candidates must show caste or tribe certificates and cut-off marks apply.
source: NCERT Social and Political Life III, Class VIII, ch.6 Confronting Marginalisation / ch.7 Public Facilities (2024-25 printing)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Class 8 'Social and Political Life III' (code 0860) is an older printing; the new Class 8 book is hees2. NCERT names only SC/ST here (OBC is a separate chapter in Class 9, which this chapter points to).

claim: Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembling peaceably and without arms; forming associations or unions (and co-operative societies); moving freely in India; residing and settling anywhere in India; practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.31 (chart) and p.35. The right to property was sub-clause (f) until 1979 (J01).

claim: Each Article 19 freedom has its own limits. Article 19(2) lets a law impose reasonable restrictions on speech in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.35 lists only 'public order, peace and morality etc.'. The 1951 and 1963 additions are shown in the Constitution's footnotes to Art. 19(2).

claim: Article 19(5) lets a law restrict movement and residence in the interest of the general public or to protect any Scheduled Tribe's interests; Article 19(6) allows restrictions on trade, including professional qualifications and State monopolies.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: The 44th Amendment (Act of 1978, in force 20 Jun 1979) omitted Art. 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) and Art. 31, and added Art. 300A: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.46 says 'in 1978, the 44th amendment'. The Act is of 1978 but came into force on 20 Jun 1979 (footnote). Also, NCERT says the 1973 Supreme Court decision held the right to property was not part of the basic structure; POL-06 (H06) found this is not stated as the Court's holding in Kesavananda: CONFLICT, see J02.

claim: Shreya Singhal (24 Mar 2015): Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down in its entirety as violating Article 19(1)(a) and not saved by Article 19(2).
source: Supreme Court of India: Shreya Singhal v Union of India, WP(Crl) 167/2012, judgment 24 Mar 2015
page_or_section: Nariman J., operative part; PDF p.101
note: Judgment by Nariman J. (two-judge bench with Chelameswar J., per the header). The Court separated discussion, advocacy and incitement (discussion and advocacy are protected). Section 79 and Section 69A were dealt with separately and are not covered here.

claim: NCERT says the government may declare an assembly of five or more persons unlawful in certain areas, which can be misused against genuine protest.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT's rule was the old Criminal Procedure Code s.144; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 replaced the CrPC from 1 Jul 2024 (our background knowledge only). The current section was not opened: UNVERIFIED for today, see open items. FOLLOW-UP 3-4 Nov 2026: BNSS text now read (X05): the current section is s.163 (urgent orders), and s.148 deals with dispersal of an assembly of five or more persons. Still date the use; the 1973 Code was not opened.

claim: Article 20 protects accused persons: no conviction except for a violation of a law in force when the act was done (and no heavier penalty than then allowed); no one is prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once; no accused person is compelled to be a witness against himself.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.36 lists these three rights in plain words.

claim: Article 21: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. NCERT Grade 9 prints this text.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
note: NCERT iest1 p.140 box prints the text; the exact printed quote is in a side box.

claim: Gopalan (1950) read the rights in Part III as separate silos. In Puttaswamy (2017), Chandrachud J. (for four judges) recorded that this 'Gopalan doctrine' was replaced by the view in Cooper and Maneka that rights overlap; Kharak Singh's reliance on the Gopalan majority was held not to be the correct position.
value: Gopalan: rights as isolated silos; later view rejected
source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
page_or_section: Part T, conclusion 2 (Chandrachud J.); Parts D, E; PDF p.261
second_source: A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras, 19 May 1950, copy on Indian Kanoon (header only checked)
note: Description of Gopalan comes from the 2017 judgment, not from reading Gopalan; Gopalan's own bench and judges not tallied. Gopalan (19 May 1950) date from the IK header. AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: the claim rests on Puttaswamy (official copy, Part T conclusion 2, para on Cooper and Maneka). The Gopalan date and bench (Kania CJ, Fazal Ali, Patanjali Sastri, Mahajan, Das, Mukherjea JJ.) are from the Indian Kanoon header only; official copy of Gopalan not read. FOLLOW-UP 3-4 Nov 2026: official copy of Gopalan read (sources/official_gopalan.pdf, api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/1251.pdf): judgment of 19 May 1950; bench Kania CJ, Fazal Ali, Patanjali Sastri, Mahajan, Das and Mukherjea JJ., matching the dates and bench given above. Kania CJ writes that 'the articles in Part III deal with different and separate rights' (PDF p.20), the basis of the 'separate silos' label. The IK caveat is closed; the other judges' views were not tallied.

claim: Maneka Gandhi (25 Jan 1978): the procedure in Article 21 must be 'right and just and fair' and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; it must pass the test of reasonableness under Article 14.
source: Supreme Court of India: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, judgment 25 Jan 1978 (seven judges)
page_or_section: Bhagwati J. opinion, 'right and just and fair' passage, official PDF p.57-58 (the headnote repeats it on p.12)
second_source: Reused: Puttaswamy Part T 3(H) repeats it
note: Bhagwati J. wrote for himself, Untwalia and Fazal Ali JJ.; Beg CJ, Chandrachud J. and Krishna Iyer J. concurred; Kailasam J. dissented. Facts: the Government impounded her passport 'in the interests of the general public' and at first gave no reasons.

claim: NCERT Grade 9 glosses 'procedure established by law' as 'strict adherence to duly enacted and valid laws'. Since Maneka Gandhi, a valid law is not enough: the procedure itself must be fair, just and reasonable.
source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: Supreme Court of India: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India, judgment 25 Jan 1978 (seven judges)
note: The NCERT gloss reflects the older Gopalan idea. Do not teach the NCERT gloss alone. The NCERT box is a side definition, not the main text.

claim: Puttaswamy (24 Aug 2017, nine judges): the Order of the Court, signed by all nine, says the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms in Part III; M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh are overruled to the extent they said otherwise. (UPSC Prelims 2024 Q76: Article 21.)
source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
page_or_section: Order of the Court, items (i)-(iv); PDF p.546
note: Answer to PYQ Prelims 2024 Q76 (options a-d: Arts 15, 16, 19, 21): (d) Article 21, with Part III freedoms as well. The Order is signed by all nine judges; Chandrachud J. delivered the judgment for four, and five others (Chelameswar, Bobde, Sapre, Nariman and Kaul JJ.) wrote separate judgments.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J. (for himself, Khehar CJI, Agrawal and Nazeer JJ.): a law that invades privacy must meet a three-fold test: legality (a law exists), a legitimate State aim (need), and proportionality (a rational link between aim and means). Privacy is not absolute.
source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
note: This is the plurality opinion for four judges; other judges' tests (for example Kaul J., Sapre J.) differ in wording and were not compared.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J.: ADM Jabalpur (1976, Emergency case on whether life and liberty can be suspended) 'must be and is accordingly overruled', along with Union of India v Bhanudas Krishna Gawde.
source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
page_or_section: Part I, 'Discordant notes', para 118ff; PDF p.120
note: Said in Chandrachud J.'s opinion for four judges; the Order of the Court does not list it. Other judges' separate opinions also criticise ADM Jabalpur (Chelameswar J., Nariman J. and others quote it); not tallied.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J.: informational privacy is part of privacy; dangers to privacy come from State and non-State actors; the Court commended to the Union Government a robust data-protection regime.
source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
note: Today's statute (the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023) was not opened; UNVERIFIED as a current position.

claim: Article 21A: the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged six to fourteen as the State may by law determine. It was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 and came into force on 1 Apr 2010.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (text blocked)
note: NCERT iest1 p.141 says the Right to Education 'was added in 2009': the Act (RTE Act) was passed in 2009, but Art. 21A is from 2002 and both started 1 Apr 2010 (the Act's own commencement not opened, indiacode 504).

claim: NCERT Grade 9 says Article 21A (Right to Education) 'was added in 2009'. The Constitution footnote shows the 86th Amendment Act was of 2002, in force 1 Apr 2010.
source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: NCERT confuses the year of the RTE Act with the year of the amendment.

claim: Olga Tellis (10 Jul 1985): Chandrachud CJ wrote that the right to life includes the right to livelihood, because no one can live without the means of living; depriving someone of livelihood would deprive them of life without any procedure.
value: livelihood is part of the right to life
source: Supreme Court of India: Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation, judgment 10 Jul 1985
page_or_section: Chandrachud CJ, para on Art. 21; PDF p.4
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: The Court still allowed removal of pavement dwellers after notice and a fair procedure (not read in full: UNVERIFIED on the exact directions). The Constitution Bench was five judges (file header lists the bench).

claim: NCERT says the Supreme Court has held that the right to shelter and livelihood are part of the right to life. Olga Tellis supports livelihood; 'shelter' as a separate holding was not found in it.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: Shelter: not found in Olga Tellis; other Supreme Court cases (not opened) are the likely source. Livelihood: CONFIRMED in D18.

claim: Article 22(1)-(2): a person arrested must be told the grounds as soon as may be, has the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, and must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding journey time).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.34. Art. 22(3) says these two clauses do not apply to enemy aliens or to people detained under a preventive detention law.

claim: Preventive detention: Article 22(4) says a preventive-detention law cannot authorise detention longer than three months unless either (a) an Advisory Board of High Court judges or persons qualified to be one reports sufficient cause before the three months end, or (b) the person is detained under a law of Parliament made under Art. 22(7)(a)-(b). Article 22(7) lets Parliament fix the cases where no Advisory Board is needed, and the longest period.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.35 states three months and the Advisory Board. The 44th Amendment (1978) would change clause (4); the footnote in the 10 Sep 2026 text says that change is 'date to be notified', so the printed text (three months) is what applies (D21b). AUDIT 3 Nov 2026 correction: the earlier wording said 'only if an Advisory Board reports', which left out clause (4)(b) and 22(7)(a). I did not look for whether Parliament has made such a law; do not say it has.

claim: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 (s.3) would change Art. 22(4) (preventive detention beyond two months needs an Advisory Board report), but the Legislative Department's footnote shows the change is still 'date to be notified', so the three-month text above is what applies.
value: 44th Amendment change to Art. 22(4) not in force
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Living fact; check the footnote again at each republish. NCERT keps2 p.35 says three months, which matches.

claim: D.K. Basu (18 Dec 1996): the Court laid down guidelines for every arrest and detention, including a memo of arrest attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, informing a relative or friend, and a diary entry at the place of detention.
source: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal, judgment 18 Dec 1996 (Kuldip Singh and A.S. Anand JJ.), Supreme Court official copy (api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/14580.pdf)
note: Judgment by Kuldip Singh J. (IK header). Court copy not reached. The number and wording of all eleven guidelines was read for items 1-7 only. AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: official copy obtained and read; the memo of arrest (attested by one witness, countersigned by the arrestee), the friend-or-relative right and the diary entry are in requirements (2), (3), (6).

claim: Article 359(1): when an Emergency is proclaimed the President may suspend the right to move a court to enforce Part III rights, except articles 20 and 21 (the exception comes from the 44th Amendment, 1978).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Supreme Court of India: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, WP(C) 494/2012, judgment 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges)
note: So after 1978 the text itself protects Arts 20 and 21; in 2017 the Court also overruled ADM Jabalpur (D14).

claim: NCERT Class 8 says 'the Constitution of India recognises the right to water as being a part of the Right to Life under Article 21'. Article 21's text does not mention water; the Supreme Court has read in the right (Subhash Kumar, 1991: pollution-free water and air).
value: water under Art. 21: by judicial reading, not by text
source: NCERT Social and Political Life III, Class VIII, ch.7 Public Facilities (2024-25 printing)
second_source: Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar, 1991 AIR 420, 1991 SCR (1) 5, judgment 9 Jan 1991, Supreme Court of India, own copy
note: NCERT hess307 p.89 (read earlier). Official copy of Subhash Kumar read 3 Nov 2026 (sources/official_subhash_kumar.pdf): bench K.N. Singh J. and N.D. Ojha J. (PDF p.1); judgment says 'Right to live is a fundamental right under Art 21 ... and it includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life' (PDF p.7; headnote HELD 1, PDF p.2). The petition was dismissed; the sentence is the Court's reading of Art. 21 while explaining when Art. 32 can be used. Art. 21's text does not mention water (verified at the Constitution). NCERT's 2007 Andhra Pradesh High Court example was not looked up.

claim: Article 23(1): traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited, and contravention is an offence punishable by law. Article 23(2) allows compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination on religion, race, caste or class.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.37.

claim: PUDR (Asiad workers, 18 Sep 1982): Bhagwati J. held that labour for less than the minimum wage is 'forced labour' under Article 23, and that Article 23 works against private contractors, not only the State.
source: People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India (Asiad workers), judgment 18 Sep 1982 (Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.), Supreme Court official copy (api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/9882.pdf)
page_or_section: headnote 5:8-5:9 and judgment text on minimum wage and Art. 23, judis PDF p.6-9
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: The Asian Games case of NCERT keps2 p.27. Bench: Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ. (IK header). Headnote text read; judgment text lines on minimum wage also seen. Court copy not reached. AUDIT 3 Nov 2026: official copy obtained and read; Bhagwati J. is the author; headnote and text agree on minimum wage and on Art. 23 against private persons.

claim: Article 24: no child below fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or in any other hazardous employment.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.38. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act (as amended, 2016) is wider than Art. 24; its text could not be opened (indiacode 504), so only the Constitution's text is claimed here. FOLLOW-UP 3-4 Nov 2026: CALPRA text now read (X03): s.3(1) bans child employment in any occupation or process, with s.3(2) exceptions; Art. 24 claim above is unchanged.

claim: NCERT Class 8 says the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act came into force on 6 December 2013, and that a PIL filed in 2003 led the Court to order checks and rehabilitation.
source: NCERT Social and Political Life III, Class VIII, ch.6 Confronting Marginalisation / ch.7 Public Facilities (2024-25 printing)
note: The Act and the Supreme Court order were not opened (indiacode 504; case not searched). Teach as 'NCERT says' only until checked.

claim: Article 25(1): subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of Part III, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. Explanation I says wearing and carrying kirpans is part of the Sikh religion.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: Article 25(2): the State may regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity linked to religion, and make laws for social welfare and reform or throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Explanation II treats references to Hindus as including Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists (same article).

claim: Article 26: every religious denomination may establish and maintain institutions, manage its own affairs in matters of religion, own and acquire property, and administer it as the law allows, subject to public order, morality and health.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: Article 27: no person can be compelled to pay taxes whose proceeds are specifically spent on promoting any particular religion. Article 28(1): no religious instruction in an institution wholly maintained out of State funds; 28(3) no one can be compelled to attend religious instruction in aided or recognised institutions.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: Venkataramana Devaru (8 Nov 1957): the Court held that a denomination's right under Art. 26(b) to exclude others from its temple yields to the public's right of entry under Art. 25(2)(b), but the two are harmonised so that the denomination's own rites remain.

claim: Bijoe Emmanuel (11 Aug 1986): children who stood respectfully but did not sing the national anthem, because of their religious faith, could not be expelled; the Court held their rights under Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1) were infringed.

source: Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala, 1987 AIR 748, 1986 SCR (3) 518, judgment 11 Aug 1986, Supreme Court of India, own copy

The headnote caveat is closed because the judgment itself was read.

claim: NCERT says the State may curb harmful practices done in the name of religion (sati, bigamy, human sacrifice are NCERT's examples) and that the Constitution gives a right to spread information about one's religion but does not allow forcible conversion.
value: limits on religion; propagation vs forced conversion

claim: The word 'secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 (in force 3 Jan 1977); NCERT keps2 says India has no official religion and the State will not favour any religion.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: NCERT Grade 8 notes that minority protections and equality can seem to conflict, and says 'some people feel' that minority protections go against secularism.

claim: Article 29(1): any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it. Article 29(2): no citizen shall be denied admission to an institution run by the State or aided by it on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: Article 30(1): all minorities, based on religion or language, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 30(2): the State shall not discriminate in aid against an institution because a minority manages it. Article 30(1A): compensation for acquisition of such an institution's property.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: The Constitution's text does not define 'minority' (searched the full 10 Sep 2026 text for a definition). NCERT describes minorities as groups with a common language or religion that are outnumbered in a part of the country or the whole.

second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: Article 32(1)-(2): the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights is itself guaranteed; the Court may issue directions, orders or writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch.5 Citizenship: Rights and Duties (First ed. June 2026)

claim: Article 226(1): every High Court can issue directions, orders or writs to any person or authority for enforcing Part III rights and for any other purpose. NCERT Grade 9 says citizens can seek remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Grade 9 Part 1, ch.6 Democracy (First ed. June 2026)

claim: Article 33 lets Parliament decide how far Part III rights apply to the armed forces and similar forces; Article 34 lets Parliament indemnify acts done to restore order where martial law was in force.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: These are the stated limits of Part III beyond the 'reasonable restrictions' in each article. Art. 33's text was not separately keyed.

claim: Article 31B: Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule are not void for inconsistency with Part III. Article 31A and 31C also protect some land and policy laws. (Details in POL-06.)
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: Reused claims POL06-F01, F06, F07 (Waman Rao, Coelho)

claim: The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 and can recommend, not prosecute. NCERT keps2 gives its composition and role.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

'Set up in 1993' rests only on the deemed commencement of 28 Sep 1993 (s.1(3)); the constitution date is not in the Act. Status left UNVERIFIED for the composition line, which is NCERT-only.

claim: Article 37: the Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, but are fundamental in the governance of the country, and it is the State's duty to apply them in making laws. Article 36 gives 'State' the same meaning as in Part III.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.43.

claim: Articles 38 and 39 set welfare goals: a social order of justice; an adequate means of livelihood for men and women; equal pay for equal work; ownership and control of resources distributed for the common good. Article 39A (free legal aid) was added by the 42nd Amendment.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.45 chart (equal pay, adequate livelihood).

source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: NCERT keps2 p.45 chart lists village panchayats under 'Policies'.

claim: Article 41: within its economic capacity the State shall make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: Article 43: the State shall endeavour to secure a living wage and decent conditions of work for workers, and to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT keps2 p.45 chart lists 'Promotion of cottage industries'.

claim: Article 44: the State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India. Article 47: the State shall regard raising nutrition and public health as primary duties and endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs, except for medicinal purposes. Article 48: organising agriculture and animal husbandry and prohibiting slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: Article 45 (substituted by the 86th Amendment, 2002): early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years; Article 50: separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: The Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights collided over land reform and property. claim: Article 51A lists eleven Fundamental Duties, (a) to (k). Part IVA and the first ten duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (in force 3 Jan 1977); duty (k), for a parent or guardian to provide education to a child aged six to fourteen, was added by the 86th Amendment (in force 1 Apr 2010).

second_source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch.5 Citizenship: Rights and Duties (First ed. June 2026)

claim: The Constitution has no clause that lets a court enforce the Fundamental Duties, and NCERT says enjoyment of rights is not made conditional on duties.

source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: NCERT Political Theory: a right is an entitlement or a justified claim, something others must recognise as a legitimate claim; not every want is a right.

second_source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch.5 Citizenship: Rights and Duties (First ed. June 2026)
note: Same idea in NCERT hees2 p.146: 'rights are justified claims'.

claim: NCERT: seventeenth- and eighteenth-century theorists said rights come from nature or God (life, liberty and property); today the term 'human rights' is used more because the idea of natural law seems unacceptable.
source: NCERT Political Theory, Class XI, ch.5 Rights (Reprint 2026-27)
note: Second source NOT FOUND: no primary text (Locke's Second Treatise, UDHR) retrieved. Teach as 'NCERT says'.

claim: NCERT: constitutional recognition gives rights special importance; rights are mainly claims on the state and place both positive and negative obligations on it (what it must do and must not do).

source: NCERT Political Theory, Class XI, ch.5 Rights (Reprint 2026-27)

claim: NCERT: democracies usually begin with political rights, then civil liberties; economic rights follow as needs are recognised; cultural rights (mother-tongue education) are also now recognised.
source: NCERT Political Theory, Class XI, ch.5 Rights (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT also mentions a 'recent' rural employment guarantee scheme (p.74): that scheme and its current legal form were not checked (UNVERIFIED, dated).

claim: NCERT: rights also place obligations on each of us, such as protecting the environment for the common good.

second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: The constitutional duties are Art. 51A (I07).

claim: NCERT: a 'bill of rights' is a list of rights protected by the constitution; the Motilal Nehru committee demanded one in 1928.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work, Class XI, ch.2 Rights in the Indian Constitution (Reprint 2026-27)
note: Second source NOT FOUND: the Nehru Report (1928) was not retrieved. Say 'NCERT says'.

claim: NCERT keps2 (p.27) opens with two real stories: construction workers at the 1982 Asian Games paid below minimum wage (the Court accepted this was forced labour), and Machal Lalung, held in judicial custody for 54 years before release in 2005.

claim: NCERT Grade 7 (Exploring Society): India is a democratic republic whose Constitution guarantees fundamental rights; the rule of the majority must not violate the rights of any citizen; elected leaders cannot pass laws against basic rights such as free speech, religion or equality before law.

second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: NCERT's 'dominance of the majority' glossary term. Supported by Art. 13(2).

claim: NCERT Grade 7: the judiciary protects the rights and liberty of citizens; if fundamental rights are violated, we can go to court.
source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 7 Part 2, ch.6 The State, the Government, and You (Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Page number from the section position; not individually checked.

claim: NCERT Grade 8: the Constitution lists six categories of fundamental rights: equality (Arts 14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), freedom of religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30), constitutional remedies (32).
source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch.5 Citizenship: Rights and Duties (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: NCERT Grade 7 explains the equality provisions: every person equal before the law (from the President to a domestic worker), no discrimination on religion, race, caste, place of birth or sex, access to public places, untouchability abolished.
source: NCERT Social and Political Life II, Class VII, ch.1 On Equality (2024-25 printing)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

claim: NCERT Grade 8 (Confronting Marginalisation): Dalits and others 'invoke' Fundamental Rights (Articles 15 and 17) to demand that the government recognise injustice and enforce the law; minorities draw on freedom of religion and cultural and educational rights.

claim: NCERT Grade 8 (Public Facilities): the government must provide public facilities (water, healthcare, schools, electricity) for everyone because private companies work for profit.

claim: NCERT Grade 8 (Citizenship): discrimination is unfair treatment on identity; inclusion is ensuring no one is left out; discrimination blocks people from enjoying fundamental rights.

claim: NCERT Grade 8: the 11th duty (parents to ensure education for children aged 6-14) was added in 2002; fundamental duties remind citizens to take an active part in keeping democracy strong.

claim: Everyday example (from NCERT, imagined): a roadside tea-shop serves a friend in an earthen cup because of his caste. Article 15(2)(a) bars any disability about access to shops and hotels on grounds of caste, and Article 17 forbids untouchability. The shopkeeper is a private person; the article says 'No citizen shall'.

claim: Everyday example: you or a relative is arrested. The police must say why, allow a lawyer, and produce you before a magistrate within 24 hours (Art. 22); under D.K. Basu they must also make a signed memo of arrest and tell a relative or friend.

claim: Everyday example: your phone, bank or health app holds your data. Puttaswamy (2017) says the right to privacy covers informational privacy and that dangers come from State and non-State actors; it asked the Union Government to create a data-protection regime.

claim: Real story: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded 'in the interests of the general public' and, at first, she was told no reasons. The reason came out only in the Government's reply to her petition. The Court held that the Article 21 procedure must be fair and just (D10).

claim: Spot the mistake: 'Article 19 freedoms belong to every person in India, including foreigners.' Correct: Article 19 says 'All citizens'; Articles 14 and 21 say 'any person' / 'No person'.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Game idea. See also NCERT hees2 p.147 'every Indian citizen' (A12).

claim: Spot the mistake: 'A government can keep someone in preventive detention for a year without any review.' Correct: beyond three months the detention needs an Advisory Board report of sufficient cause (Art. 22(4)(a)), unless a law of Parliament under Art. 22(7) says otherwise (22(4)(b)); the detained person must also be told the grounds and given the earliest chance to make a representation (Art. 22(5)).
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Game idea. Subject to the Parliament's power under Art. 22(7).

claim: Spot the mistake: 'An Ordinance is not a law, so it can override a Fundamental Right.' Correct: Art. 13(3)(a) counts an Ordinance as a law, and Art. 13(2) bars laws that abridge Part III rights.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Game idea. Prelims 2025 tested this.

claim: Spot the mistake: 'Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights at all.' Correct: it can, but not so as to alter the basic structure (Kesavananda, 1973; seven judges on that question).
source: Supreme Court of India, Basic Structure Judgment site: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (SCR text), reused from POL-06
second_source: Reused POL06-D04
note: Game idea; details in POL-06.

claim: Common question: 'Do Fundamental Rights apply against private persons?' Answer from the text: some are addressed to 'the State' (Arts 14, 15(1), 16), while Art. 15(2), Art. 17, Art. 23 and Art. 24 are not limited to the State; PUDR (1982) held Art. 23 works against private contractors.
source: People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India (Asiad workers), judgment 18 Sep 1982 (Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.), Supreme Court official copy (api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/9882.pdf)
page_or_section: Art. 23 discussion (enforceable against private individuals), judis PDF p.9-10
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Our summary of which articles are not addressed to the State alone is an inference from the article texts; other Fundamental Rights against private actors (for example Kaushal Kishor, 2023) were not opened.

claim: Common question: 'Is reservation itself a Fundamental Right?' Not settled in the sources read. Art. 16(4) says nothing shall prevent the State from reserving; the lead judgment in Indra Sawhney calls it part of equality, not an exception.
source: Indra Sawhney v Union of India, judgment 16 Nov 1992 (nine judges), copy of the Supreme Court Reports text on Indian Kanoon (court copy not reached)
note: Mukesh Kumar v State of Uttarakhand (2020), which is usually cited for 'no fundamental right to reservation', was not opened. Do not state it as the Court's holding yet.
